The compression curve can also be plotted using axial strain instead of void ratio. For plots using strain, the compression parameters are Cεc and Cεr (instead of Cc and Cr). The strain or void ratio used in plotting the compression curve can either be the value at the end of the time increment or the value at the end of primary consolidation. It is important that the method used is indicated for the plot.

If a 24-hour load cycle is used for the incremental stress consolidation test, the test can take two to three weeks to complete, depending on the value of the maximum stress and the number of unload-reload loops. Laboratories often try to decrease the amount of time required by reloading the test specimen at the end of primary (EOP) consolidation as opposed to constant time intervals. If the test is conducted using an automated apparatus, the time corresponding to EOP is often determined by a computer program. The use of computer-calculated EOP times may incur errors, especially for low stresses where strains are small. If the test specimen is reloaded too quickly at early stages of the test, the remaining data may not be useable and the quality of the test may be compromised.
key_points: Standard specimen: 2.5-in diameter, 1-in height; confined in a rigid ring for one-dimensional (vertical) compression only.
Fixed-ring consolidometer is most common; floating-ring reduces friction effects for soils like sandy clay.
Load Increment Ratio (LIR) = Δσ/σ0; LIR=1 doubles the load; LIR=-0.75 for unloading; LIR=4 for reloading.
Compression curve (e-log p) yields preconsolidation pressure σʹp, compression index Cc, and recompression index Cr.
Coefficient of consolidation (cv) is determined from the time-deformation curve for each load increment.
24-hour load cycles can make the test take 2–3 weeks; end-of-primary (EOP) loading can shorten duration.
Automated EOP detection may introduce errors at low stresses; premature reloading can compromise test quality.

equations.description: Load Increment Ratio (LIR) defined as the change in applied stress divided by the initial total stress: LIR = Δσ / σ0

sections.applicability: Applies when performing or interpreting incremental loading one-dimensional consolidation tests on fine-grained, partially saturated, compacted, or remolded soils per ASTM D2435.

sections.title: Constant Rate of Strain Consolidation Test (ASTM D4186)
sections.summary: Describes the Constant Rate of Strain (CRS) consolidation test (ASTM D4186) as an alternative to incremental loading. Covers back-pressure saturation requirements, single-drainage configuration with pore pressure measurement at the base, strain rate selection criterion (excess pore pressure ≤15% of applied stress), and advantages including a continuous compression curve with improved preconsolidation pressure resolution and cv determination over the full load range.
sections.body:
The constant rate of strain (CRS) consolidation test (ASTM D4186 – Standard Test Method for One-Dimensional Consolidation Properties of Saturated Cohesive Soils Using Controlled-Strain Loading) can be used as an alternative to the incremental stress consolidation test. The test specimens for the CRS test are the same size as for the incremental stress tests. One of the main advantages of the CRS test is that the compression curve can be obtained in much less time than the incremental stress test. A schematic of the basic test elements and the data acquired is given in Figure 3-14.

The CRS consolidation test can be conducted on intact soil specimens, and also on compacted and remolded soil specimens. However, it is necessary that the test specimen be saturated prior to compression. As shown in Figure 3-14, the consolidometer for the CRS test is very similar to a triaxial cell. The test specimen is back-pressure saturated in the same manner as a triaxial specimen. The cell pressure applied in the cell serves as back pressure in the process. The test specimen is drained only at the top, and during the loading process, the excess pore water pressures are measured at the bottom. Based on an assumed parabolic distribution of pore water pressure in the test specimen, the average effective stress can be calculated.

The test specimen is loaded at a constant strain rate (ε). The strain rate is selected such that the excess pore water pressure measured at the base of the test specimen does not exceed 15% of the applied stress. The rate for unloading the test specimen is much slower than loading, and unload-reload loops may slow down the test considerably.

One advantage of the CRS consolidation test is that the compression curve is defined by many more data points than the incremental stress consolidation test. There are so many data points taken that the results are usually portrayed as a curve instead of discrete data points. This allows an increased resolution of the compression curve in the vicinity of the preconsolidation pressure, and allows a more accurate determination of its value. The CRS consolidation test also allows the determination of the coefficient of consolidation (cv) over the entire load range as long as the excess pore pressures are in an acceptable range. This method of determining cv removes some of the subjectivity involved in determining cv using time curves with the incremental stress consolidation test.
key_points: CRS test (ASTM D4186) is faster than incremental loading (D2435) and yields a continuous compression curve.
Specimen must be fully saturated prior to compression; back-pressure saturation is used in a triaxial-like cell.
Drainage is single-ended (top only); excess pore pressure is measured at the base to compute average effective stress.
Strain rate is selected so that base excess pore pressure does not exceed 15% of applied stress.
Continuous data points provide better resolution near the preconsolidation pressure σʹp.
cv can be determined over the entire load range, reducing subjectivity compared to time-curve methods.
Unload-reload loops are slower than loading and can considerably extend test duration.
sections.applicability: Applies when using the CRS consolidation test as a faster alternative to incremental loading for saturated cohesive soils requiring high-resolution compression curves or full-range cv determination.

sections.title: Swell and Collapse Test (ASTM D4546)
sections.summary: Describes the one-dimensional swell or collapse test (ASTM D4546) used for partially saturated natural or compacted soils that swell or collapse upon wetting. Covers free swell measurement (typically under 20 psf nominal stress), swell pressure determination, and the procedure of applying loads then inundating the specimen to measure volume change as a function of stress at inundation. Uses the same consolidometer as D2435.
sections.body:
When a partially saturated natural soil or a compacted soil is given access to water, the soil can swell at low stresses or collapse at high stresses. ASTM D4546 (Standard Test Methods for One-Dimensional Swell or Collapse of Soils) allows the volume change of the test specimen to be measured as a function of the applied stress. If the soil has no confining stress applied, then free swell may occur. Often, free swell is measured under a nominal stress of 20 psf. If the pressure is varied to prevent any swell or volume change from occurring, this pressure is called the swell pressure for the soil. ASTM D4546 allows the amount of free swell, swell pressure, and volume change for other stresses to be determined.

The test is very similar to an incremental stress consolidation test, and the same consolidometer is used. Loads can be applied to the test specimen, and after the test specimen has achieved equilibrium under the load, the specimen is inundated. The swell or collapse volume change is measured after the test specimen achieves a new equilibrium. Shown in Figure 3-15 is an example curve that gives the volume change of the soil as a function of the stress at inundation.
key_points: ASTM D4546 measures one-dimensional swell or collapse of partially saturated natural or compacted soils upon wetting.
Soils can swell at low stresses or collapse at high stresses when given access to water.
Free swell is typically measured under a nominal stress of 20 psf when no confining stress is applied.
Swell pressure is the stress required to prevent any volume change upon inundation.
Uses the same consolidometer as the incremental loading consolidation test (ASTM D2435).
Volume change vs. stress-at-inundation curve is the primary output (see Figure 3-15).
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the swell or collapse potential of partially saturated natural or compacted soils that will be exposed to water under field conditions.

sections.title: Expansion Index Test (ASTM D4829)
sections.summary: Describes the ASTM D4829 Expansion Index Test for assessing swell potential of compacted soils. Unlike D4546, it does not yield engineering design values but provides a simple index (EI = % swell × 10) to evaluate swelling risk for structures built on compacted fill, using criteria in Table 3-7.
sections.body: The expansion index test (ASTM D4829 – Standard Test Method for Expansion Index of Soils) determines the swell potential of a soil, but it is less rigorous than D4546. It does not provide engineering design values to calculate volume change, but provides a simple index to assess the swelling potential of soil. This test is conducted on compacted soils. The main use of the expansion index test is to assess if a compacted fill might pose problems if structures are constructed on top of it. The compaction mold is approximately half the height of the 4-inch diameter (1/30 ft3) compaction mold used for ASTM D698 and the same compaction hammer as used for D698 is used. The goal is to compact the test specimen using a D698 effort at a degree of saturation of 50%. A vertical stress of 1 psi is applied, and the specimen is allowed to equilibrate for 10 minutes. The specimen is then inundated and allowed to swell for 24 hours or until the swell has essentially ceased. The Expansion Index (EI) is equal to the percent swell multiplied by 10. The expansion potential is assessed using the criteria shown in Table 3-7.
key_points: ASTM D4829 is a simpler, less rigorous alternative to D4546; it does not yield engineering design values for volume change calculations.
Test is conducted on compacted soils; primary use is assessing swelling risk for structures on compacted fill.
Specimen is compacted to a D698 effort at 50% degree of saturation; 1 psi vertical stress applied for 10-minute equilibration.
Specimen is inundated and swell measured for 24 hours or until swell ceases.
Expansion Index (EI) = percent swell × 10; classified from Very Low (EI 0–20) to Very High (EI >130) per Table 3-7.
sections.applicability: Applies when a simple index of swell potential is needed for compacted soils, particularly for evaluating compacted fill beneath structures.

sections.title: Hydraulic Conductivity (Permeability) Tests
sections.summary: Introduces the history and general framework of hydraulic conductivity testing in soils. Notes that permeability tests have been in use since the 1930s, that correlations are more reliable for coarse-grained soils, and that two ASTM standardized tests exist, with hydraulic conductivity also derivable from consolidation tests.
sections.body: Test to measure the permeability or hydraulic conductivity of soils have been used since the 1930s. In general, permeability tests have been more widely used for fine-grained soils as opposed to coarse-grained soils. There are many correlations available for the permeability of coarse-grained soils, but few reliable correlations exist for fine-grained soils. Currently, there are two ASTM standardized tests for hydraulic conductivity. However, hydraulic conductivity can be calculated from incremental stress and constant rate of strain consolidation tests.
key_points: Hydraulic conductivity testing has been practiced since the 1930s.
Many correlations exist for coarse-grained soils; few reliable correlations exist for fine-grained soils.
Two ASTM standardized tests are available for hydraulic conductivity measurement.
Hydraulic conductivity can also be derived indirectly from incremental stress and constant rate of strain (CRS) consolidation tests.
sections.applicability: Applies as an introductory overview whenever hydraulic conductivity testing is being selected or discussed for any soil type.

sections.title: Compaction Mold Test (ASTM D5856)
sections.summary: Describes ASTM D5856, a rigid-wall permeameter test intended for compacted soils with hydraulic conductivity less than 10⁻³ cm/sec. Notes key deficiencies including inability to saturate specimens (resulting in potentially underestimated conductivity) and risk of side-wall leakage; best suited as a QC test for compacted clay liners.
sections.body:
The compaction mold test (ASTM D5856 – Standard Test Method for Measurement of Hydraulic Conductivity of Porous Material using a Rigid-Wall Compaction-Mold Permeameter) is intended to be used on compacted soils having a hydraulic conductivity less than 10-3 cm/sec.

This test has a major deficiency in that the test specimen cannot be saturated, therefore the measured hydraulic conductivity may be too low. There also is a problem that leakage can occur between the compacted test specimen and the wall of the compaction mold. This test is best suited as a quality control test for compacted clay liners for landfills and reservoirs.
key_points: ASTM D5856 uses a rigid-wall compaction-mold permeameter; applicable for soils with hydraulic conductivity < 10⁻³ cm/sec.
Major deficiency: specimens cannot be fully saturated, so measured hydraulic conductivity may be underestimated.
Side-wall leakage between specimen and mold wall is a known problem.
Best suited as a quality control test for compacted clay liners in landfills and reservoirs.
sections.applicability: Applies when performing quality control hydraulic conductivity testing on compacted clay liners for landfills and reservoirs, where k < 10⁻³ cm/sec.

sections.title: Flexible Wall Test (ASTM D5084)
sections.summary: Describes ASTM D5084, the most common permeability test, using a flexible membrane (triaxial permeameter) that eliminates side-wall leakage, allows back-pressure saturation, and controls effective consolidation stress. Recommended for soils with k < 10⁻⁴ cm/sec; supports intact, remolded, and compacted specimens and can measure hydraulic conductivity anisotropy.
sections.body:
The flexible wall test (ASTM D5084 – Standard Test Methods for Measurement of Hydraulic Conductivity of Saturated Porous Materials Using a Flexible Wall Permeameter) is the most common permeability test. The apparatus used is also called a triaxial permeameter because it is essentially a triaxial cell without the loading rod. The sample is enclosed in a flexible membrane, therefore the problem of side-wall leakage experienced in D5856 is not a problem. The membrane conforms to irregularities in the sides of the test specimen. ASTM D5084 also allows for test specimens to be back-pressure saturated in the same manner as CU and CD triaxial test specimens. The flexible wall permeability test also allows control of the effective consolidation stress. This is not possible with the compaction mold test.

This method is recommended only for soils having a hydraulic conductivity less than 10-4 cm/sec, so it is best suited to fine-grained soils or soils with a significant percentage of fines. Intact, remolded, and compacted test specimens can be used for this test. The test takes considerable skill to properly conduct, and there are six different methods to promote flow though the test specimen. The test measures vertical hydraulic conductivity, but intact samples can be trimmed at different orientations to measure anisotropy of hydraulic conductivity.
key_points: ASTM D5084 is the most common permeability test; apparatus is a triaxial cell without a loading rod (triaxial permeameter).
Flexible membrane eliminates side-wall leakage problems present in the rigid-wall D5856 test.
Back-pressure saturation is possible, same as for CU and CD triaxial tests.
Effective consolidation stress can be controlled — an advantage over the compaction mold test.
Recommended for soils with k < 10⁻⁴ cm/sec; best suited to fine-grained soils or soils with significant fines.
Intact, remolded, and compacted specimens are all permissible; six flow-promotion methods are available.
Anisotropy of hydraulic conductivity can be evaluated by trimming intact samples at different orientations.
sections.applicability: Applies when measuring hydraulic conductivity of fine-grained or fines-rich soils (k < 10⁻⁴ cm/sec) requiring saturation control and minimized side-wall leakage.

sections.title: Hydraulic Conductivity from Consolidation Tests
sections.summary: Introduces the method of deriving hydraulic conductivity indirectly from consolidation tests via the coefficient of consolidation (cv). For incremental stress consolidation tests, cv is obtained from time curves using various methods; for CRS consolidation tests, cv is calculated directly from test output. This section is introductory and continues beyond the chunk.
sections.body: One of the purposes of conducting a consolidation test is to determine the coefficient of consolidation (cv). For incremental stress consolidation tests, cv is calculated from the time curves using one of several different methods. For the CRS consolidation test, cv
key_points: Hydraulic conductivity can be derived indirectly from consolidation tests via the coefficient of consolidation (cv).
For incremental stress consolidation tests, cv is calculated from time-settlement curves using one of several methods.
For CRS (constant rate of strain) consolidation tests, cv is computed directly from test measurements.
sections.applicability: Applies when hydraulic conductivity is to be estimated indirectly from consolidation test data, particularly for fine-grained soils.

sections.title: Laboratory Tests on Rock
sections.summary: Introduces ASTM laboratory tests applicable to rock specimens, noting the smaller number of rock tests compared to soils. Most common rock tests focus on compressive and tensile strength. Lists four key ASTM standards (D3967, D5607, D5731, D7012) covering splitting tensile strength, direct shear, point load index, and compressive strength/elastic moduli of intact rock core specimens.
sections.body: ASTM also addresses laboratory tests on rock specimens, but there are much fewer tests for rocks than for soils. Most of the common tests on rock focus on the strength in compression and tension. Table 3-8 lists the common rock tests that have ASTM standards available.
key_points: Fewer ASTM laboratory tests exist for rock than for soils; most focus on compressive and tensile strength.
Key ASTM rock standards include D3967 (splitting tensile), D5607 (direct shear), D5731 (point load index), and D7012 (compressive strength and elastic moduli).
Parameters obtained include σt (tensile strength), c-φ/c'-φ' (shear strength), Is/Is(50) (point load index), and σu (unconfined compressive strength).
D5607 strength parameters are mainly interpreted as total stress values.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting laboratory test methods for rock specimens per ASTM standards.

sections.title: Unconfined Compression Test (ASTM D7012)
sections.summary: Describes ASTM D7012 for compressive strength and elastic moduli of intact rock cores. Covers four test methods, two for unconfined compressive strength (Method C) and two for triaxial compression. Method C yields only σu without axial strain measurement. Specimens are typically 1.85-inch diameter NQ cores trimmed to ≥3.7-inch height, loaded to failure in 2–15 minutes. Multiple specimens are tested due to variability from joints, fractures, and faults.
sections.body:
ASTM D7012 (Standard Test Methods for Compressive Strength and Elastic Moduli of Intact Rock Core Specimens under Varying States of Stress and Temperatures) encompasses more than just unconfined compression tests. There are four different methods of testing outlined in the standard, and two address the unconfined compressive strength. The other two address triaxial compression of rock, which is used less frequently than for soil.

The basic form of the unconfined compression test (Method C) does not measure axial strain during loading, and provides only the unconfined compressive strength. The resulting strength can be used for design or as an index property for the rock. The test is normally conducted on rock cores that are 1.85 inches in diameter, and they are trimmed to be at least 3.7 inches in height. This specimen diameter corresponds to an NQ core barrel, but larger rock cores can be used as well. The specimen can be loaded at a constant rate of load or a constant rate of strain which are chosen to cause failure in 2 minutes to 15 minutes. Unconfined compression tests of rock are normally conducted on many test specimens since there can be wide variations in the compressive strength due to the effects of planes of weakness (joints, fractures, and faults) and other inhomogeneities in rock. The main result of the unconfined compression test is the uniaxial compressive strength (σu).
key_points: ASTM D7012 includes four methods: two for unconfined compressive strength and two for triaxial compression of rock.
Method C (basic unconfined compression) yields only σu — no axial strain is measured during loading.
Standard specimen size is 1.85 inches diameter (NQ core barrel) × ≥3.7 inches height (minimum 2:1 height-to-diameter ratio).
Loading rate is selected to cause failure within 2 to 15 minutes.
Multiple specimens are typically tested due to high variability caused by joints, fractures, faults, and other inhomogeneities.
Result σu can be used directly for design or as a rock index property.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the uniaxial compressive strength and/or elastic moduli of intact rock core specimens.

sections.title: Split Cylinder Test (ASTM D3967)
sections.summary: Covers the ASTM D3967 split cylinder (Brazilian) test as an alternative to direct tensile testing of rock. The specimen is loaded diametrically between hardened steel platens; thickness ranges from 0.2 to 0.75 times the diameter. Failure is achieved in 1–10 minutes. Main result is splitting tensile strength (σt). Results are variable, so multiple specimens are routinely tested; results are conventionally distinguished from direct tension values by the 'splitting' prefix.
sections.body: The split cylinder test (ASTM D3967 – Standard Test Method for Splitting Tensile Strength of Intact Rock Core Specimens) is used as an alternative to the direct tensile test. The test specimen is loaded diametrically via hardened steel end platens. The test specimen thickness can range between 0.2 to 0.75 times the specimen diameter. The test specimen is loaded at a rate sufficient to obtain failure in 1 to 10 minutes. The main result of this test is the splitting tensile strength (σt). Although the tensile strength resulting from the split cylinder test should be essentially equal to that measured from direct tension tests, it is customary to preface the former with "splitting." Owing to the variability in the test results, split cylinder tests are often run on numerous test specimens.
key_points: The split cylinder test is a practical alternative to direct tensile testing of intact rock cores.
Specimen is loaded diametrically between hardened steel platens; thickness = 0.2–0.75× specimen diameter.
Loading rate targets failure in 1 to 10 minutes.
Primary result is splitting tensile strength (σt), conventionally distinguished from direct tension by the 'splitting' prefix.
High variability in results requires testing numerous specimens.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the tensile strength of intact rock core specimens as an alternative to direct tension testing.

sections.title: Rock Direct Shear Test (ASTM D5607)
sections.summary: Describes ASTM D5607 for direct shear strength of rock specimens and discontinuities under constant normal force. Unlike the soil counterpart, the rock direct shear test is treated as undrained. Tests are run over a range of normal stresses to define the strength envelope. Specimens are typically encapsulated in super-strength gypsum cement. Apparatus must accommodate extreme load/displacement ranges: up to 50,000 lbs and displacements from <0.01 inch (intact rock) to >0.1 inch (rock joints at low normal stress).
sections.body:
Rock direct shear tests (ASTM D5607 - Standard Test Method for Performing Laboratory Direct Shear Strength Tests of Rock Specimens Under Constant Normal Force) can be conducted on intact rock specimens, as well as on joints and discontinuities. Unlike the direct shear test conducted on soils, the rock direct shear test is normally considered to be an undrained test. The basic elements of this test are the same as for the soil direct shear tests. Rock direct shear tests are often conducted for a range of normal stresses to determine the strength envelope for the material. One major difference is that the test specimen is often encapsulated in a super strength gypsum cement to fix its position in the shear box.

Rock direct shear tests are more complicated than the soil counterpart because of the great variety of loads and displacements the apparatus is required to measure. For large normal stresses, it can take 50,000 lbs. to fail an intact rock direct shear test specimen, and failure may occur at very small (<0.01 inch) displacements. For rock joints at low normal stresses, the failure load might be less than 100 lbs., and the displacement at failure may be greater than 0.1 inch.
key_points: Applicable to intact rock specimens and to joints/discontinuities under constant normal force.
Unlike soil direct shear, the rock test is normally treated as an undrained test.
Tests are conducted over a range of normal stresses to define the shear strength envelope (c-φ or c'-φ').
Specimens are often encapsulated in super-strength gypsum cement to fix position in the shear box.
Apparatus must handle wide load ranges: up to ~50,000 lbs for intact rock and as low as <100 lbs for rock joints.
Failure displacements range from <0.01 inch (intact rock at high normal stress) to >0.1 inch (joints at low normal stress).
sections.applicability: Applies when determining direct shear strength of intact rock, rock joints, or discontinuities under constant normal force.

sections.title: Point Load Test (ASTM D5731)
sections.summary: Introduces the ASTM D5731 point load test for determining a rock strength index (Is or Is(50)). The test can be performed on rock cores or irregular rock pieces with diameters from 1 to 3 inches. Load platens are truncated cones with a 0.2-inch-radius semicircular arc tip. Specimen diameter is defined as the distance between platen contact points. The index is commonly corrected to a standard 50 mm specimen diameter.
sections.body: The point load test (ASTM D5731 – Standard Test Methods for Determination of the Point Load Strength Index of Rock and Application of Rock Strength Classifications) provides an index value of the rock strength. This test can be performed on rock cores or irregular pieces of rock having diameters in the range of 1 inch to 3 inches. A photograph of the point load apparatus is shown in Figure 3-18. The diameter of the test specimen is considered to be the thickness of the test specimen from loading platen contact points. The load platens are truncated cones, with the point being a semicircular arc of 0.2-inch radius.
key_points: Provides a strength index (Is or Is(50)) rather than a direct strength measurement; index is often corrected to 50 mm specimen diameter.
Applicable to rock cores or irregular rock pieces with diameters ranging from 1 to 3 inches.
Specimen diameter is defined as the distance between the truncated-cone platen contact points.
Load platens are truncated cones with a semicircular arc tip of 0.2-inch radius.
Versatile field and laboratory test useful for rock strength classification.
sections.applicability: Applies when an index of rock strength is needed for classification purposes, using rock cores or irregular rock specimens.

sections.title: OTHER SOIL AND ROCK TESTS
sections.summary: Briefly notes that while the chapter covers the most common geotechnical tests used in U.S. practice, hundreds of additional ASTM standardized tests exist. These include test groups addressing partially saturated soils, soil-cement mixtures, peats and organic soils, geosynthetics, and other engineering materials not covered in detail in this chapter.
sections.body: This section of the manual has addressed the tests that are the most common in geotechnical engineering practice in the U.S., but there are hundreds of other ASTM standardized tests. There are groups of tests that address partially saturated soils, soil-cement mixtures, peats and organic soils, geosynthetics, and many other materials used in engineering projects.
key_points: The chapter focuses on the most common geotechnical tests used in U.S. practice, but is not exhaustive.
Hundreds of additional ASTM standardized tests exist beyond those covered in this chapter.
Additional test groups cover partially saturated soils, soil-cement mixtures, peats and organic soils, geosynthetics, and other engineering materials.
Engineers should consult ASTM standards directly for specialized materials or conditions not addressed in this chapter.
sections.applicability: Applies when an engineer needs to identify geotechnical or materials testing beyond the common tests covered in Chapter 3, particularly for specialized materials such as partially saturated soils, soil-cement, peats, or geosynthetics.

sections.title: Suggested Reading
sections.summary: Provides an annotated bibliography of key references for Chapter 3 topics, organized by subject area: General Laboratory Testing (Head, Lambe & Whitman), Shear Strength (ASTM STP 361, STP 740, ASCE conference proceedings, Saada & Townsend), and Triaxial Testing (ASTM STP 977, Bishop & Henkel, Lade). Essential for engineers seeking deeper technical grounding beyond the UFC.
sections.body:
Topic: General Laboratory Testing
Head, K. H. 2008. Manual of Soil Laboratory Testing, Vol. 1., 3rd Ed., Whittles, 416 pp.
Head, K. H. and R. J. Epps 2011. Manual of Soil Laboratory Testing Vol. II, Permeability Shear Strength, and Compressibility Tests, 3rd Ed., Whittles, 512 pp.
Head, K. H. and R. J. Epps 2014, Manual of Soil Laboratory Testing Vol. III, Effective Stress Tests, 3rd Ed., Whittles, 448 pp.
Lambe, T. W. and R. V. Whitman 1969. Soil Mechanics, John Wiley and Sons, Inc. 553 pp.

Topic: Shear Strength
Laboratory Shear Testing of Soils, ASTM STP 361, American Society for Testing and Materials, 505 pp., 1964.
Laboratory Shear Strength of Soils, ASTM STP 740, R. N. Young and F. C. Townsend, Eds., 717 pp, 1981.
Research Conference on Shear Testing of Cohesive Soils, ASCE, University of Colorado, Boulder, CO, 1164 pp, 1960.
Saada, A. S. and Townsend, F. C. 1981. "State of the Art: Laboratory Strength Testing of Soils," Laboratory Shear Strength of Soils, ASTM STP 740, R. N. Yong and F. C. Townsend, Eds., ASTM, pp. 7-77.

Topic: Triaxial Testing
Advanced Triaxial Testing of Soil and Rock, ASTM SPT 977, Robert T. Donague, Ronald C. Chaney, and Marshal L. Silver, Eds., American Society for Testing and Materials, Philadelphia, 896 pp, 1988.
Bishop, A. W. and D. J. Henkel (1957), Measurement of Soil Properties in the Triaxial Test, Edward Arnold, Ltd., London, 190 pp.
Lade, P. 2016. Triaxial Testing of Soils, John Wiley & Sons, Ltd., 500 pp.
key_points: Three-volume Head & Epps series covers all major laboratory soil testing topics: basic testing, permeability/shear/compressibility, and effective stress tests.
Lambe & Whitman 'Soil Mechanics' (1969) is a foundational general reference for soil behavior and testing.
ASTM STP 361 and STP 740 are key compiled references for laboratory shear strength testing methods and data.
Saada & Townsend (1981) provides a state-of-the-art review of laboratory strength testing as of the early 1980s.
Bishop & Henkel (1957) remains a seminal reference for triaxial testing procedures and soil property measurement.
Lade (2016) is the most recent comprehensive triaxial testing reference listed, covering modern practice.
sections.applicability: Applies when an engineer needs supplemental reading on general laboratory testing, shear strength testing, or triaxial testing beyond the UFC content.

sections.title: Notation
sections.summary: Defines all symbols and abbreviations used throughout Chapter 3, covering soil index properties (e, Gs, n, S, w), unit weights (γd, γt, γsat, γb, γw), consolidation parameters (Cc, Cr, cv, mv, Pp, σʹp, σʹv), strength parameters (c, cʹ, φ, φʹ, su), compaction parameters (Dr, RC, γd-max, γd-min, wopt), stress/strain variables (σ0, σ3, Δσ, ε, τcyc), and point load index values (Is, Is(50)).
sections.body:
Symbol | Description
c | Total stress cohesion
Cc | Compression index
Cr | Recompression index
cv | Coefficient of consolidation
cʹ | Effective stress cohesion
D | Diameter
Dr | Relative density
e | Void ratio
emax | Maximum index void ratio
emin | Minimum index void ratio
Gs | Specific gravity
H | Height
Is | Uncorrected point load strength index
Is(50) | Size corrected point load strength index
k | Hydraulic conductivity or permeability
K0 | At-rest earth pressure coefficient
L | Length
mv | Coefficient of volumetric compressibility
n | Porosity
Pp | Maximum past pressure
RC | Relative compaction
S | Degree of saturation
St | Sensitivity
su | Undrained shear strength for a φ = 0 envelope for saturated soils
t | Thickness
V | Total volume
Va | Volume of air
Vs | Volume of solids
Vv | Volume of voids
Vw | Volume of water
w | Water content
wopt | Optimum water content
Ws | Weight of solids
Wt | Total weight of sample
Ww | Weight of water
γb | Buoyant unit weight or submerged unit weight
γd | Dry unit weight
γd-max | Maximum dry density from the compaction curve for a particular effort or maximum index dry density (corresponding to emin)
γd-min | Minimum index dry density (corresponding to emax)
γt | Total or wet unit weight
γsat | Saturated unit weight
γw | Unit weight of water
∆σ | Change in applied stress
ε | Strain rate
σ0 | Initial total stress
σ3 | Confining pressure
σʹp | Preconsolidation pressure
σʹv | Vertical effective consolidation stress
τcyc | Applied peak cyclic shear stress
φ | Total stress friction angle
φʹ | Effective stress friction angle
key_points: Distinguishes total stress (c, φ) from effective stress (cʹ, φʹ) cohesion and friction angle — critical for correct strength analysis.
su is specifically defined as undrained shear strength for a φ = 0 envelope for saturated soils, not a general undrained strength symbol.
Relative density (Dr) and relative compaction (RC) are both listed, reflecting their distinct roles in compaction and density characterization.
γd-max corresponds to emin and γd-min corresponds to emax, linking compaction density limits to void ratio extremes.
Consolidation parameters include Cc, Cr, cv, mv, Pp, σʹp, and σʹv, covering both settlement magnitude and rate calculations.
Point load index appears in both uncorrected (Is) and size-corrected (Is(50)) forms, consistent with ASTM point load testing procedures.
τcyc is included as applied peak cyclic shear stress, indicating the chapter addresses dynamic/cyclic loading conditions.
Volume phase relationship variables (V, Va, Vs, Vv, Vw) and weight variables (Ws, Wt, Ww) provide a complete phase diagram symbol set.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever a symbol used in Chapter 3 requires definition or clarification during design calculations or document review.
